name: git init
shortDescription: Create an empty Git repository or reinitialize an existing one. This is the very first command you run when starting a new project with Git.
detailedDescription:
The `git init` command creates a new `.git` subdirectory in your current working directory. This subdirectory contains all the necessary repository metadata — the object store, refs, template files, and an initial `HEAD` file pointing to the yet-to-be-created default branch. No files are tracked yet; you must explicitly add them with `git add`.

If you run `git init` in a directory that already contains a `.git` folder, it will **not** overwrite existing configuration. Instead, it will re-initialize templates and can be used safely to pick up newly added templates or to move a repository to another location.

The `.git` directory is what makes a folder a Git repository. If you delete it, you lose all version history. Everything Git knows about your project lives inside this single hidden folder.

parameters.description: If provided, Git will create a new directory with this name and initialize the repository inside it. If omitted, the current directory is used.
Use the specified name for the initial branch instead of the configured default. Since Git 2.28, the default branch name is configurable. Many teams now use `main` instead of `master`.
Creates a bare repository — one without a working directory. Bare repos are used as centralized remotes (like what GitHub hosts). You cannot edit files or make commits directly in a bare repo.
Specifies a directory from which templates will be copied into the new `.git` directory. Templates let you pre-configure hooks, exclude patterns, and other defaults.
Specifies that the repository is shared among several users. This allows users belonging to the same group to push into that repository. Can be `group`, `all`, `world`, or an octal number.

examples.title: Initialize a new project
examples.description: The most common usage. Navigate to your project folder and run git init. This creates the .git directory and you're ready to start tracking files.
examples.code:
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
git init

# Output:
# Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/you/my-project/.git/

examples.title: Initialize with main as default branch
examples.description: Many teams and platforms (GitHub, GitLab) now use 'main' as the default branch. Use -b to set this from the start rather than renaming later.
examples.code:
git init -b main

# This avoids having to do:
#   git branch -m master main
# after the first commit.

examples.title: Set default branch name globally
examples.description: Instead of passing -b every time, configure Git to always use 'main' as the default branch for all new repositories.
examples.code:
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Now every 'git init' will use 'main' automatically

examples.title: Create a bare repository for a team server
examples.description: Bare repositories have no working directory — they only store Git data. This is what remote servers like GitHub use internally.
examples.code:
git init --bare /srv/repos/team-project.git

# Team members can now clone from this:
# git clone user@server:/srv/repos/team-project.git

commonMistakes.text: Running `git init` inside an existing repo will NOT destroy your history. It's safe but rarely needed. If you see 'Reinitialized existing Git repository', nothing was lost.
Never run `git init` in your home directory (`~`) or a very high-level folder. Git will try to track everything underneath, leading to massive, unusable repositories.
If you're joining an existing project, you almost certainly want `git clone`, not `git init`. Use `git init` only when starting a brand new project from scratch.
